questions.question: Can you describe a project or assignment where you designed and built a data pipeline using Python and SQL? Please include details about the data sources, transformations, and how you ensured data quality.
Tell me about a time when you had to troubleshoot a failed data pipeline under time pressure. How did you identify the issue, and what steps did you take to resolve it?

answers.question: Can you describe a project or assignment where you designed and built a data pipeline using Python and SQL? Please include details about the data sources, transformations, and how you ensured data quality.

transcription.text: Sure. Last semester, I built a data pipeline for a university project that tracked live football match statistics. We had three different data sources, a live scores API, a separate player statistics API and ACSV export from our own database. And my job was to get all of that into one clean Postgresql database that the rest of the team could query for the dashboard. The biggest challenge came about two weeks in. The Live Scores API would occasionally send a match event twice, a few seconds apart, and if I wasn't careful my pipeline would insert it as two separate goals instead of one. I only noticed because the numbers on our dashboard didn't match the real match reports, which was embarrassing to catch late. So I went back and wrote a proper test suite around the ingestion logic before I touched anything else. I wrote tests that fed in duplicate events on purpose and asserted the database only ended up with one row, and I added a unique constraint on the event ID as a second line of defense in case the application logic ever missed a case. I also wrote a small script that ran nightly and cross-checked our totals against the official match reports so we would catch a mismatch automatically instead of a teammate noticing weeks later. The other thing I had to do was explain this to our team lead, who wasn't technical. I didn't want to just say there was a bug in the deduplication logic because that means nothing to someone who doesn't write code. Instead I told her it was like two people texting her the same score update, and if you don't check whether you've already heard that news, you end up double counting it. That framing actually helped, because she then understood why I wanted to spend an extra day on tests instead of just moving on to the next feature. By the end, the pipeline was processing about 10,000 events a day with zero duplicate incidents in the four weeks before we submitted, and the nightly reconciliation script gave the team confidence that if something did break, we would know within a day rather than finding out from a confused user. It taught me that testing data pipelines properly means testing for the messy real-world cases, not just the happy path, and that being able to explain a technical problem simply is honestly as important as fixing it
